claim: XBP1u is a mammalian protein containing a functionally critical translational arrest peptide (AP).
source: XBP1u, a central component of the unfolded protein response (UPR), is a mammalian protein containing a functionally critical translational arrest peptide (AP).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of XBP1u.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the stalled human XBP1u AP has a resolution of 3 Å.
source: Here, we present a 3 Å cryo-EM structure of the stalled human XBP1u AP.
evidence: The resolution is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in the results.

claim: The XBP1u AP forms a unique turn in the ribosomal exit tunnel proximal to the peptidyl transferase center.
source: It forms a unique turn in the ribosomal exit tunnel proximal to the peptidyl transferase center where it causes a subtle distortion, thereby explaining the temporary translational arrest induced by XBP1u.
evidence: This structural observation is stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM data shown in figures.

claim: The XBP1u AP causes a subtle distortion at the peptidyl transferase center.
source: It forms a unique turn in the ribosomal exit tunnel proximal to the peptidyl transferase center where it causes a subtle distortion, thereby explaining the temporary translational arrest induced by XBP1u.
evidence: The distortion is described in the abstract and detailed in structural analysis.

claim: During ribosomal pausing, the hydrophobic region 2 (HR2) of XBP1u is recognized by SRP.
source: During ribosomal pausing the hydrophobic region 2 (HR2) of XBP1u is recognized by SRP, but fails to efficiently gate the Sec61 translocon.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM structures of XBP1u-RNC-SRP complexes.

claim: HR2 of XBP1u fails to efficiently gate the Sec61 translocon.
source: During ribosomal pausing the hydrophobic region 2 (HR2) of XBP1u is recognized by SRP, but fails to efficiently gate the Sec61 translocon.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural observations showing Sec61 in the idle state.

claim: Only 8 out of 20 mutagenized positions in the XBP1u AP are optimal.
source: An exhaustive mutagenesis scan of the XBP1u AP revealed that only 8 out of 20 mutagenized positions are optimal; in the remaining 12 positions, we identify 55 different mutations increase the level of translational arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by saturation mutagenesis data in Figure 6.

claim: 55 different mutations in 12 positions of the XBP1u AP increase the level of translational arrest.
source: An exhaustive mutagenesis scan of the XBP1u AP revealed that only 8 out of 20 mutagenized positions are optimal; in the remaining 12 positions, we identify 55 different mutations increase the level of translational arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis data presented in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The wildtype XBP1u AP induces only an intermediate level of translational arrest.
source: Thus, the wildtype XBP1u AP induces only an intermediate level of translational arrest, allowing efficient targeting by SRP without activating the Sec61 channel.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis data showing many mutations increase arrest potency.

claim: Arrest peptides can induce ribosomal stalling to regulate gene expression.
source: Polypeptide stretches, which can induce ribosomal stalling to regulate gene expression, are called ribosomal arrest peptides (AP).
evidence: This is a general statement about arrest peptides in the introduction, representing established knowledge.

claim: Arrest peptides traverse through the ribosomal tunnel and establish stable contacts with the tunnel wall.
source: While being synthesized as a nascent chain, they traverse through the ribosomal tunnel and establish stable contacts with the tunnel wall.
evidence: This describes the general mechanism of arrest peptides, representing established knowledge.

claim: Arrest peptides distort the peptidyl transferase center and inhibit further peptide bond formation.
source: This eventually distorts one of the ribosomal active site, usually the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), and inhibits further peptide bond formation (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claim: Some arrest peptides require external co-effector molecules to exert their function.
source: In some cases the capacity of APs to stall translation is not only dependent on the AP sequence but also requires an external co-effector molecule, such as arginine and tryptophan in the case of arginine attenuator peptide AAP (Wang and Sachs, 1997) and TnaC leader peptide (Gong and Yanofsky, 2002), to exert its function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Sachs, 1997 and Gong and Yanofsky, 2002.

claim: Several bacterial arrest peptides stall independently of any additional small molecules.
source: In contrast, several bacterial APs stall independently of any additional small molecules, yet, are sensitive to pulling force on the nascent chain, thereby serving as force sensors (SecM [secretion monitor], MifM, VemP [Vibrio export monitoring peptide] [Butkus et al., 2003; Chiba et al., 2009; Ishii et al., 2015; Ismail et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Butkus et al., 2003; Chiba et al., 2009; Ishii et al., 2015; Ismail et al., 2012.

claim: Arrest peptides can inhibit translation during elongation.
source: Depending on the context APs can inhibit translation during elongation (SecM, VemP) (Ishii et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2014), termination (TnaC, CMV uORF2 (cytomegalovirus upstream open reading frame 2) and SAM-DC uORF (S-adenosyl-methionine decarboxylase) (Gong et al., 2001; Janzen et al., 2002; Raney et al., 2002) or both in some cases (ErmCL, MifM and AAP) (Chiba and Ito, 2012; Fang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ishii et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: Arrest peptides can inhibit translation during termination.
source: Depending on the context APs can inhibit translation during elongation (SecM, VemP) (Ishii et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2014), termination (TnaC, CMV uORF2 (cytomegalovirus upstream open reading frame 2) and SAM-DC uORF (S-adenosyl-methionine decarboxylase) (Gong et al., 2001; Janzen et al., 2002; Raney et al., 2002) or both in some cases (ErmCL, MifM and AAP) (Chiba and Ito, 2012; Fang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2001; Janzen et al., 2002; Raney et al., 2002.

claim: Some arrest peptides have a defined stall position.
source: Properties of these APs also vary in a way that some have a defined stall position (Ishii et al., 2015), while others have multiple stalling sites (Chiba and Ito, 2012; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: Some arrest peptides have multiple stalling sites.
source: Properties of these APs also vary in a way that some have a defined stall position (Ishii et al., 2015), while others have multiple stalling sites (Chiba and Ito, 2012; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chiba and Ito, 2012; Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of arrest peptides within the ribosomal tunnel have provided structural and mechanistic insights.
source: Cryo-EM structures of these APs within the ribosomal tunnel provided further structural and mechanistic insights, and also enabled visualization of their unique conformation and interactions, which explain their ability to inhibit ribosomal translation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: No structural consensus of arrest peptides has been observed.
source: Strikingly, apart from establishing contacts with the ribosomal tunnel mostly between the PTC and the tunnel constriction formed by the ribosomal proteins uL4 and uL22, no structural consensus of APs has been observed (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claim: Arrest peptide structures range from entirely extended conformation to almost entirely folded in secondary structure.
source: To the contrary, so far the structures range from an entirely extended conformation (Zhang et al., 2015) to almost entirely folded in secondary structure (Matheisl et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015; Matheisl et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017.

claim: Most arrest peptide structures characterize prokaryotic APs, with the exception of CMV uORF2.
source: Until now, most structures characterize prokaryotic APs, with the exception of ribosomal termination stalling mediated by CMV uORF2 (Matheisl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matheisl et al., 2015.

claim: UPR represents the central cellular response mechanism that alleviates endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: UPR represents the central cellular response mechanism that alleviates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and adjusts ER activity levels (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: In mammalian cells, UPR is mainly mediated by three transmembrane sensors: IRE1α, ATF6, and PERK.
source: In mammalian cells, this pathway is mainly mediated by three transmembrane sensors that are located in the ER membrane: inositol requiring enzyme one alpha (IRE1α), activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), and pancreatic endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK) (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: IRE1 is the evolutionarily most conserved UPR sensor.
source: Of these three sensors, the evolutionarily most conserved is IRE1 (here, IRE1 denotes mammalian IRE1α and/or yeast Ire1); in lower eukaryotes such as yeast, it is the only known sensor mediating the UPR (Mori, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mori, 2009.

claim: In yeast, IRE1 is the only known sensor mediating the UPR.
source: Of these three sensors, the evolutionarily most conserved is IRE1 (here, IRE1 denotes mammalian IRE1α and/or yeast Ire1); in lower eukaryotes such as yeast, it is the only known sensor mediating the UPR (Mori, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mori, 2009.

claim: Increasing levels of misfolded proteins during ER stress sequester BiP away from IRE1α, leading to formation of an active dimer.
source: Increasing levels of misfolded proteins during ER stress sequester BiP away from IRE1α, leading to formation of an active dimer (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Okamura et al., 2000) which is further activated by cluster formation (Aragón et al., 2009; Credle et al., 2005; Kimata et al., 2007; Korennykh et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bertolotti et al., 2000; Okamura et al., 2000.

claim: IRE1α dimer is further activated by cluster formation.
source: Increasing levels of misfolded proteins during ER stress sequester BiP away from IRE1α, leading to formation of an active dimer (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Okamura et al., 2000) which is further activated by cluster formation (Aragón et al., 2009; Credle et al., 2005; Kimata et al., 2007; Korennykh et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aragón et al., 2009; Credle et al., 2005; Kimata et al., 2007; Korennykh et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010.

claim: In yeast, direct binding of unfolded proteins to the luminal core regions of IRE1-dimer or -oligomer is required for activation.
source: In yeast, direct binding of unfolded proteins to the luminal core regions of IRE1-dimer or -oligomer is required for the activation (Gardner and Walter, 2011; Kimata et al., 2007), however, in mammals, direct binding model has been a matter of debate (Kohno, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gardner and Walter, 2011; Kimata et al., 2007.

claim: In mammals, the direct binding model for IRE1α activation has been a matter of debate.
source: In yeast, direct binding of unfolded proteins to the luminal core regions of IRE1-dimer or -oligomer is required for the activation (Gardner and Walter, 2011; Kimata et al., 2007), however, in mammals, direct binding model has been a matter of debate (Kohno, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kohno, 2010.

claim: Activated IRE1α splices XBP1u mRNA on the ER membrane, producing XBP1s mRNA.
source: The cytosolic domain of activated IRE1α then splices the XBP1u (X-box binding protein-1 unspliced) mRNA on the ER membrane, producing XBP1s (spliced) mRNA, which codes for an active transcription factor.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism in the UPR pathway.

claim: The splicing reaction involves removal of a 26-nt intron from XBP1u mRNA.
source: The splicing reaction involves removal of a 26-nt intron from XBP1u mRNA, which leads to a translational frame-shift and the replacement of C-terminal segment in XBP1u downstream of the splicing site (Calfon et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Calfon et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2001.

claim: XBP1s transcription factor activates genes encoding ER-resident chaperones and folding enzymes.
source: Once translocated to the nucleus, the XBP1s transcription factor activates genes encoding ER-resident chaperones and folding enzymes, the components of ER associated protein degradation and the proteins that function in secretory pathway, which together increase ER size and activity (Figure 1) (Shaffer et al., 2004; Sriburi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shaffer et al., 2004; Sriburi et al., 2004.

claim: XBP1u has two hydrophobic domains, HR1 and HR2.
source: XBP1u has two hydrophobic domains, HR1 and HR2, and a C-terminal AP of about 26 residues which pauses the translating ribosome when residing in the ribosomal exit tunnel (Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009.

claim: XBP1u has a C-terminal arrest peptide of about 26 residues.
source: XBP1u has two hydrophobic domains, HR1 and HR2, and a C-terminal AP of about 26 residues which pauses the translating ribosome when residing in the ribosomal exit tunnel (Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009.

claim: The XBP1u arrest peptide pauses the translating ribosome when residing in the ribosomal exit tunnel.
source: XBP1u has two hydrophobic domains, HR1 and HR2, and a C-terminal AP of about 26 residues which pauses the translating ribosome when residing in the ribosomal exit tunnel (Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yanagitani et al., 2011; Yanagitani et al., 2009.

claim: During translational pause, HR2 is exposed outside the ribosome exit tunnel and can recruit SRP.
source: During this temporary pause in translation, HR2 is exposed outside the ribosome exit tunnel and can recruit the signal recognition particle (SRP) (Kanda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kanda et al., 2016.

claim: The paused XBP1u-RNC is targeted to the Sec61 protein-conducting channel on the ER membrane.
source: As a result, the paused XBP1u ribosome-nascent-chain mRNA complex (XBP1u-RNC) is targeted to the Sec61 protein-conducting channel on the ER membrane, where mRNA splicing by IRE1α is now possible (Kanda et al., 2016; Plumb et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanda et al., 2016; Plumb et al., 2015.

claim: Translational pausing is required for efficient recruitment of SRP by the stabilized XBP1u-RNC.
source: Given the moderate hydrophobicity of HR2, translational pausing is required for efficient recruitment of SRP by the stabilized XBP1u-RNC, and is critical for proper IRE1α-mediated UPR (Kanda et al., 2016; Plumb et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanda et al., 2016; Plumb et al., 2015.

claim: A mutant version of XBP1u (S255A) pauses ribosomes more efficiently than wildtype XBP1u.
source: We structurally characterized the paused ribosomal complex (XBP1u-RNC) by cryo-EM and single particle analysis using a mutant version of XBP1u (S255A, full length numbering), which was shown previously to pause ribosomes more efficiently than wildtype XBP1u (Yanagitani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yanagitani et al., 2011.

claim: The XBP1u-RNC preparation yielded 4.2 pmol of complex.
source: The preparation yielded 4.2 pmol of XBP1u-RNC which was then used to make cryo-EM grid.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental procedure.

claim: A total of 531,952 ribosomal particles were obtained from cryo-EM dataset processing.
source: Processing of the cryo-EM dataset yielded a total of 531,952 ribosomal particles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and multiple rounds of in silico sorting for homogenous populations resulted in ~60% of programmed ribosomes (Figure 2B), with the major population of ribosomes in the non-rotated state (~42%, P- and E- site tRNA) and a minor population in the rotated, not yet fully translocated state (~18%, A/P- and P/E- site tRNA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Approximately 60% of ribosomes were programmed after in silico sorting.
source: Processing of the cryo-EM dataset yielded a total of 531,952 ribosomal particles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and multiple rounds of in silico sorting for homogenous populations resulted in ~60% of programmed ribosomes (Figure 2B), with the major population of ribosomes in the non-rotated state (~42%, P- and E- site tRNA) and a minor population in the rotated, not yet fully translocated state (~18%, A/P- and P/E- site tRNA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The major population of ribosomes (~42%) is in the non-rotated state with P- and E-site tRNA.
source: Processing of the cryo-EM dataset yielded a total of 531,952 ribosomal particles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and multiple rounds of in silico sorting for homogenous populations resulted in ~60% of programmed ribosomes (Figure 2B), with the major population of ribosomes in the non-rotated state (~42%, P- and E- site tRNA) and a minor population in the rotated, not yet fully translocated state (~18%, A/P- and P/E- site tRNA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: A minor population of ribosomes (~18%) is in the rotated state with A/P- and P/E-site tRNA.
source: Processing of the cryo-EM dataset yielded a total of 531,952 ribosomal particles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and multiple rounds of in silico sorting for homogenous populations resulted in ~60% of programmed ribosomes (Figure 2B), with the major population of ribosomes in the non-rotated state (~42%, P- and E- site tRNA) and a minor population in the rotated, not yet fully translocated state (~18%, A/P- and P/E- site tRNA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The average resolution of the post state paused complex is 3.0 Å.
source: The average resolutions of the paused complexes were 3.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) for the post state and 3.1 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) for the rotated hybrid state, respectively, with the ribosomal core reaching a resolution of 2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The average resolution of the rotated hybrid state paused complex is 3.1 Å.
source: The average resolutions of the paused complexes were 3.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) for the post state and 3.1 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) for the rotated hybrid state, respectively, with the ribosomal core reaching a resolution of 2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The ribosomal core reaches a resolution of 2.5 Å.
source: The average resolutions of the paused complexes were 3.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) for the post state and 3.1 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) for the rotated hybrid state, respectively, with the ribosomal core reaching a resolution of 2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: A major portion of the XBP1u peptide in the exit tunnel was resolved to between 3.0–3.5 Å for both classes.
source: A major portion of the XBP1u peptide in the exit tunnel was resolved to between 3.0–3.5 Å for both classes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B), whereas the resolution in the part distal to the PTC near the exit was worse than 4 Å, apparently due to flexibility of the nascent chain.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: 24 amino acid residues of XBP1u were modeled, covering the entire AP.
source: We could model 24 amino acid residues of XBP1u, covering the entire AP.
evidence: This is a result from molecular modeling of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Ribosomes are paused with Met260 connected to the tRNA in the P-site.
source: In both states, we observed that the ribosomes are paused with Met260 connected to the tRNA in the P-site, in full agreement with findings from ribosome-profiling analysis of mouse embryonic cells (Ingolia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and citation to Ingolia et al., 2011.

claim: The majority of the visible XBP1u nascent chain adopts an extended conformation.
source: The majority of the visible XBP1u nascent chain adopts an extended conformation, except in the proximity of the PTC where the AP forms a prominent turn in the tunnel (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The turn in the XBP1u AP is comprised of eight residues from W249 to W256.
source: The turn is comprised of eight residues from W249 to W256, and involves the C-terminal half of the characterized XBP1u AP.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The beginning of the turn is only four residues away from the PTC.
source: Notably, the beginning of the turn is only four residues away from the PTC, suggesting that the turn within the tunnel may be critical for the pausing activity of XBP1u.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Six of the eight turn-forming residues have been previously shown to be critical for pausing by alanine scanning mutagenesis.
source: Of the eight turn-forming residues, six have been previously shown to be critical for pausing by alanine scanning mutagenesis (Yanagitani et al., 2011), c.f., below.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yanagitani et al., 2011.

claim: Residue 255 (A255) is part of the turn and is tightly packed in the structure.
source: Interestingly, residue 255 that has been mutated from Ser to Ala in the sequence used here is part of the turn: A255 is tightly packed in the structure and the larger Ser residue may be sterically more problematic, possibly explaining why the S255A mutation makes the XBP1u a stronger AP.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The S255A mutation makes XBP1u a stronger arrest peptide possibly because the larger Ser residue may be sterically more problematic.
source: Interestingly, residue 255 that has been mutated from Ser to Ala in the sequence used here is part of the turn: A255 is tightly packed in the structure and the larger Ser residue may be sterically more problematic, possibly explaining why the S255A mutation makes the XBP1u a stronger AP.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: The turn is located in close proximity to the PTC, above the constriction at uL22 and uL4.
source: The turn is located in close proximity to the PTC, above the constriction at uL22 and uL4, the narrowest portion of the tunnel.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The conformation of the XBP1u peptide in the distal parts of the tunnel is similar to that observed for a non-pausing mammalian nascent chain.
source: The conformation of the XBP1u peptide in the distal parts of the tunnel is similar to that observed for a non-pausing mammalian nascent chain in the mammalian ribosome (Voorhees and Hegde, 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–D) and to other known viral and bacterial APs (CMV, MifM and VemP, Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-G) (Matheisl et al., 2015; Sohmen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with cited structures.

claim: The turn observed for XBP1u is unique and is located in a part of the tunnel where some other APs adopt α-helical secondary structure.
source: However, the turn observed for XBP1u is unique, and is located in a part of the tunnel where some other APs adopt α-helical secondary structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-G).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other arrest peptides.

claim: The turn in the XBP1u AP is framed by two tryptophan residues (W249 and W256).
source: The turn in the XBP1u AP makes several key interactions with the tunnel wall and is in part in close proximity to the PTC. It is framed by two tryptophan residues (W249 and W256) and protrudes into a hydrophobic crevice in the tunnel, causing the displacement of the base G3904 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The XBP1u turn protrudes into a hydrophobic crevice in the tunnel, causing the displacement of the base G3904.
source: The turn in the XBP1u AP makes several key interactions with the tunnel wall and is in part in close proximity to the PTC. It is framed by two tryptophan residues (W249 and W256) and protrudes into a hydrophobic crevice in the tunnel, causing the displacement of the base G3904 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The base corresponding to G3904 in prokaryotes (A2058) constitutes the A-stretch in E. coli ribosome which is critical for macrolide binding and drug-mediated ribosome stalling.
source: The corresponding base in prokaryotes, A2058, constitutes, together with A2059, the so-called A-stretch in the E. coli ribosome which is critical for macrolide binding and drug-mediated ribosome stalling (Wilson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson, 2009.

claim: In TnaC mediated translational arrest, the hydrophobic crevice is proposed to play a critical role in recognizing free L-tryptophan in the ribosomal exit tunnel.
source: Moreover, in TnaC mediated translational arrest the hydrophobic crevice is proposed to play a critical role in recognizing free L-tryptophan in the ribosomal exit tunnel (Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martínez et al., 2014.

claim: The positively charged side chain of Arg251 in XBP1u forms a stabilizing salt bridge with the phosphate of A4388.
source: The positively charged side chain of Arg251 in XBP1u forms a stabilizing salt bridge with the phosphate of A4388 (Figure 3F), whereas Gly250 and Gln253 engage in hydrogen bonds with A3908 and U4555, respectively (Figure 3G,I).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Gly250 and Gln253 engage in hydrogen bonds with A3908 and U4555, respectively.
source: The positively charged side chain of Arg251 in XBP1u forms a stabilizing salt bridge with the phosphate of A4388 (Figure 3F), whereas Gly250 and Gln253 engage in hydrogen bonds with A3908 and U4555, respectively (Figure 3G,I).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3G and 3I.

claim: Trp249 stacks internally onto Gln248 of XBP1u.
source: Finally, Trp249 stacks internally onto Gln248 of XBP1u, and the backbone carbonyl of Arg251 makes a hydrogen bond to Lys257 within the XBP1u nascent chain (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The backbone carbonyl of Arg251 makes a hydrogen bond to Lys257 within the XBP1u nascent chain.
source: Finally, Trp249 stacks internally onto Gln248 of XBP1u, and the backbone carbonyl of Arg251 makes a hydrogen bond to Lys257 within the XBP1u nascent chain (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Lys257 stacks onto U4532.
source: Lys257 also stacks onto U4532, and this stacking interaction might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The stacking interaction between Lys257 and U4532 might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531.
source: Lys257 also stacks onto U4532, and this stacking interaction might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Five of the eight residues that constitute the turn engage in contacts with the tunnel.
source: Taken together, five of the eight residues that constitute the turn engage in contacts with the tunnel.
evidence: This is a summary of structural observations.

claim: Tyr241 of XBP1u stacks with C2794 of 28S rRNA.
source: In the distal part of the tunnel, Tyr241 of XBP1u stacks with C2794 of 28S rRNA (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Arg71 and Ser87 of uL4, as well as Arg128 of uL22 make contacts mostly with the backbone of the nascent chain.
source: Three of the remaining interactions of the nascent chain in the distal tunnel region are mediated by the constriction proteins uL4 and uL22, respectively. Here, Arg71 and Ser87 of uL4, as well as Arg128 of uL22 make contacts mostly with the backbone of the nascent chain (Figure 3J - L).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3J-L.

claim: U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) is in its canonical upward conformation in the XBP1u-stalled RNC.
source: In contrast to some bacterial APs, we observed U4531 (U2585) in the XBP1u-stalled RNC in its canonical upward conformation.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: U4531 interacts with the side chain of Met260 but appears not to be hindered from switching downwards upon A-site accommodation.
source: Although it interacts with the side chain of Met260 (Figure 3C), it appears that this base would not be hindered to switch downwards upon A-site accommodation to adopt the induced conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: C4398 (C2452) is in the closed conformation in the XBP1u-stalled RNC.
source: However, another nucleotide, C4398 (C2452), is in the closed conformation (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a position that under normal conditions is observed only after A-site accommodation, as in the reconstruction of the yeast 80S ribosome with A-, P-site tRNA and eIF5a (PDB 5GAK) (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C4398 is stabilized in the closed conformation by Leu259.
source: C4398 (C2452) is stabilized in the closed conformation by Leu259, which, in contrast to Met260, cannot be mutated to alanine without almost entirely loosing stalling activity (see below).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by mutagenesis data.

claim: C4398 (C2452) has been implicated in A-site tRNA accommodation and peptidyl transferase activity.
source: Notably, this base has been implicated in A-site tRNA accommodation and peptidyl transferase activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of this base.

claim: The premature positioning of C4398 in the closed conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation.
source: Therefore, the premature positioning of C4398 (C2452) in the closed conformation due to its interaction with Leu259 in an unusual conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation: Leu259 would simply clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Leu259 would clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA.
source: Therefore, the premature positioning of C4398 (C2452) in the closed conformation due to its interaction with Leu259 in an unusual conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation: Leu259 would simply clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Inhibition or delay of tRNA accommodation into the A-site appears to be the main mechanism for translational pausing by the XBP1u AP.
source: Therefore, inhibition or delay of tRNA accommodation into the A-site appears to be the main mechanism for translational pausing by the XBP1u AP.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: No stable class of ribosomes carrying a canonical A-site tRNA was found in the population of stalled RNCs.
source: This idea is further supported by the observation that we do not find a stable class of ribosomes in our population of stalled RNCs that carry a canonical A-site tRNA.
evidence: This is an observation from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: A substantial fraction of the RNCs is in the rotated state.
source: Moreover, it can be easily imagined how pulling force applied to the nascent chain can rectify the only mildly perturbed geometry of the PTC and thereby alleviate stalling. Since we detect a substantial fraction of the RNCs in the rotated state (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) we cannot exclude that the XBP1u structure may also perturb translocation as well as preventing rapid A-site tRNA accommodation.
evidence: This is observed in cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No perturbation of the P-tRNA 3'-CCA end pairing with the P-loop in 28S rRNA was observed.
source: However, we do not observe any perturbation of the P-tRNA 3'-CCA end pairing with the P-loop in 28S rRNA, as was seen in other cases (Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure, contrasted with cited cases.

claim: The entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure.
source: Taken together, the entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure and, facilitated by this structure, stabilizing the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The XBP1u AP stabilizes the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
source: Taken together, the entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure and, facilitated by this structure, stabilizing the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The final reconstruction of XBP1u-RNC-SRP had an average resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: The final reconstruction had an average resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and the SRP itself was resolved between 5–10 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: SRP was resolved between 5–10 Å in the XBP1u-RNC-SRP structure.
source: The final reconstruction had an average resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and the SRP itself was resolved between 5–10 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: A clear rod-like density resembling a signal sequence was observed in the hydrophobic groove of the SRP54 M-domain.
source: Analysis of the hydrophobic groove of the SRP54 M-domain, which is known to mediate the recognition and binding of canonical signal sequences, revealed a clear rod-like density resembling that of a signal sequence (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rod-like density in the SRP54 M-domain likely represents the SRP-bound HR2 domain.
source: Since the only sufficiently hydrophobic peptide stretch available is HR2 of XBP1u, it is highly likely that this density indeed represents the SRP-bound HR2 domain, bound in a conformation indistinguishable from that of normal SRP-bound signal sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and the known composition of the complex.

claim: The exposed HR2 domain on the paused XBP1u-RNC forms a helical structure upon successful SRP recruitment.
source: Hence, we conclude that the exposed HR2 domain on the paused XBP1u-RNC forms a helical structure upon successful SRP recruitment, which makes a canonical interaction with the M-domain of SRP54.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The conformation of the AP is identical in the presence of SRP to that of the RNC alone.
source: Notably, the nascent chain density was sufficiently well resolved within the tunnel of the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complex to allow for molecular model building. At the given resolution, the conformation of the AP is identical in the presence of SRP to that of the RNC alone.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: SRP binding to paused XBP1u-RNCs does not lead to perturbation of the nascent chain within the tunnel.
source: The finding that SRP binding to paused XBP1u-RNCs does not lead to perturbation of the nascent chain within the tunnel strongly suggests that this state maintains the RNC in the paused state.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The XBP1u-RNC-Sec61 complex represents the idle state with the lateral gate of the translocon in a closed conformation.
source: When comparing with known structures of Sec61, we found that our structure represented the idle state with the lateral gate of the translocon, mainly formed by TM2 and TM7, in a closed conformation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the cryo-EM structure with known Sec61 structures, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No additional density for the HR2 domain of XBP1u was identified on or near the Sec61 complex.
source: We could not identify any additional density for the HR2 domain of XBP1u on or near the Sec61 complex, indicating a rather weak or transient interaction.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Less than 10% of XBP1u becomes integrated into the ER membrane.
source: Considering the low hydrophobicity of the HR2 domain and previous biochemical evidence that less than 10% of XBP1u becomes integrated into the ER membrane (Plumb et al., 2015), our data are in full agreement with the idea that HR2 can interact with, but cannot productively engage and gate, the Sec61 translocon.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plumb et al., 2015.

claim: The structure of the XBP1u nascent chain in the XBP1u-RNC-Sec61-complex is indistinguishable from the structures observed in the XBP1u-RNC and the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complexes.
source: The structure of the XBP1u nascent chain in the XBP1u-RNC-Sec61-complex is indistinguishable from the structures observed in the XBP1u-RNC and the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complexes, with RMSDs between the structures in the range of about 1 Å (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane.
source: This finding strongly suggests that there is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane, and XBP1u is therefore unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: XBP1u is unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
source: This finding strongly suggests that there is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane, and XBP1u is therefore unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: The long linker length of 52 amino acids between the HR2 domain and the arrest peptide prevents potential force transmission.
source: Probably the long linker length of 52 amino acids between the HR2 domain and the arrest peptide prevents any potential force applied to HR2 upon interaction with SRP or Sec61 to be transmitted to the XBP1u AP.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: Mutations P254→[V,I,C], Q253→N, and C247→[N, K] have fFL values < 0.5.
source: Particularly strong reductions in fFL were seen for mutations P254→[V,I,C], Q253→N, and C247→[N, K], that all have fFL values < 0.5.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Eight residues in the wildtype XBP1u AP are optimal for efficient translational arrest under a strong pulling force.
source: Eight residues in the wildtype XBP1u AP are optimal for efficient translational arrest under a strong pulling force (i.e., all mutations lead to an increase in fFL): Y241, P244, W249 to H252, W256, and P258.
evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Five of the eight turn residues are optimal for translational arrest.
source: Not surprisingly, the turn region W249-W256 stands out: five of the eight turn residues are optimal for translational arrest.
evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments.

claim: P244 makes a hydrogen bond to R71 in uL4.
source: P244 makes a hydrogen bond to R71 in uL4 (Figure 3J) that may be weakened if the highly constrained backbone geometry of P244 is not maintained, and Y241 makes an apparently important stacking interaction with C2794 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3J.

claim: 55 mutations in Q242, P243, F245, L246, C247, Q248, Q253, P254, S255, K257, L259, and M260 lead to reduced fFL values.
source: In contrast, some residues in the wildtype AP are clearly sub-optimal in terms of arrest potency, and we find no less than 55 mutations in Q242, P243, F245, L246, C247, Q248, Q253, P254, S255, K257, L259, and M260 that lead to reduced fFL values (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutation of C247 to charged or polar residues increases the stalling strength.
source: Mutation of C247 to charged or polar residues increases the stalling strength. These residues presumably interact with the ribosomal tunnel by forming hydrogen bonds or salt-bridges with the phosphate backbone of rRNA, but the precise interactions cannot be easily predicted from the structure.
evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments, with inference about mechanism.

claim: Mutating Q253 to Asn leads to strong increase in the translational arrest.
source: Q253 is part of the turn, and mutating it to Asn leads to strong increase in the translational arrest.
evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Nine mutations in P254 increase the stalling strength.
source: Nine mutations in the neighboring residue P254 also increase the stalling strength, albeit to varying levels.
evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The XBP1u turn is similar to a β-turn, but does not satisfy all the geometrical parameters.
source: The XBP1u turn is similar to a β-turn, but does not satisfy all the geometrical parameters and therefore is probably less stable than a canonical β-turn.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Proline is not favored in β-turns.
source: Proline is not favored in β-turns, and its presence in the turn of the XBP1u nascent chain might be a result of evolution favoring weaker translational pausing instead of a highly efficient arrest.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about β-turn structure and inference about evolutionary selection.

claim: The mutagenesis data is entirely consistent with the evolutionary conservation of the XBP1u AP.
source: The mutagenesis data is entirely consistent with the evolutionary conservation of the XBP1u AP, as seen in the Logo plot in Figure 6E.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing mutagenesis data with evolutionary conservation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: None of the sequence variants in the natural XBP1u APs lead to a strong decrease in fFL.
source: None of the sequence variants in the natural XBP1u APs lead to a strong decrease in fFL according to Figure 6C (the maximal decrease is from fFL = 0.89 to fFL = 0.52 for C247H) and, to the extent that they have been tested, none of the sequence variants in the natural APs (except S255) lead to a strong increase in fFL according to Figure 6D (the maximal increase is from fFL = 0.46 to fFL = 0.61 for P244A and R251P).
evidence: This is a result from comparing natural variants with mutagenesis data in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: S255 is completely conserved despite the fact that the S255A mutant has much stronger arrest potency.
source: It is especially noteworthy that S255 is completely conserved despite the fact that the S255A mutant has much stronger arrest potency (Figure 6D), and that the strong Q253N mutation has not been seen so far in a natural sequence.
evidence: This is observed from evolutionary conservation data and mutagenesis results in Figure 6D.

claim: The XBP1u AP is under selective pressure to maintain a rather weak translational arrest efficiency.
source: We conclude that, although the turn region in the XBP1u AP includes many residues that are optimal for translational pausing, the XBP1u AP is under selective pressure to maintain a rather weak translational arrest efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and evolutionary conservation data.

claim: The XBP1u AP carrying mutations S255A and P254C reduces fFL values throughout the force profile while the shape of the profile persists.
source: To evaluate the possible use of mutant XBP1u APs in such contexts, we re-measured the force profile in Figure 6B using a strong XBP1u AP carrying the mutations S255→A and P254→C (blue curve in Figure 6B; see Supplementary file 2 for sequences). fFL values are reduced throughout, while the shape of the profile persists.
evidence: This is a result from force profile measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The P254C mutation reduces the AP's sensitivity to both high and low pulling forces.
source: The P254C mutation thus reduces the APs sensitivity to both high and low pulling forces (i.e., both at the peak around L = 40–45 residues and at L ≥ 55 residues), suggesting that results obtained under high pulling forces (e.g., Figure 6C and D) can be extrapolated to the low-force situation that presumably applies when the XBP1u AP performs its normal function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on force profile data.

claim: No crosslinked product is apparent when a gel is run under non-reducing conditions for the P254C mutant.
source: Because the mutant AP has a Cys residue in position 254, we considered that the enhanced arrest potency may be due to the formation of a disulfide bond with a ribosomal protein, or within the nascent chain itself. However, no crosslinked product is apparent when a gel is run under non-reducing conditions, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, and fFL is even slightly reduced (as expected from Figure 6C) when the other Cys residue in the AP (C247) is mutated to Ser, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The early peak at L ≈ 30 residues seen for the SecM AP in E. coli is not clearly seen in the mammalian force profiles.
source: Interestingly, the early peak at L ≈ 30 residues seen for the same H-segment constructs expressed in E. coli with the SecM AP (Ismail et al., 2012) (gray curve, Figure 6B) is not clearly seen in the mammalian force profiles, suggesting that the H segment interacts differently with the Sec61 and SecYEG translocons at early stages of membrane insertion.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing force profiles, with citation to Ismail et al., 2012.

claim: XBP1u functions in a unique manner compared to previously described arrest peptides.
source: As with previously described APs, XBP1u apparently functions in a unique manner.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: PTC bases U4531 (U2585), U4452 (U2506) and A4548 (A2602) are known to be critical in translation elongation and termination.
source: PTC bases which are known to be critical in translation elongation and termination are U4531 (U2585), U4452 (U2506) and A4548 (A2602) and, consequently, these bases are often perturbed by APs to inactivate ribosomes (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claim: U4531 (U2585) is the most often distorted base by arrest peptides.
source: Among these, the most often distorted base is U4531 (U2585) which needs to be precisely positioned for both peptide bond formation and nascent chain release (Schmeing et al., 2005; Youngman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmeing et al., 2005; Youngman et al., 2004.

claim: XBP1u functions similarly to some arrest peptides by preventing A-site tRNA accommodation, but in a unique manner.
source: Therefore, compared to previously described APs, XBP1u functions similarly to some of them by preventing A-site tRNA accommodation (Arenz et al., 2014; Sohmen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017), however, in a unique manner (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison, with citations to Arenz et al., 2014; Sohmen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017.

claim: The saturation mutagenesis experiments demonstrate that the XBP1u AP has not evolved to maximize its resistance to pulling forces on the nascent chain.
source: It was known before that mutation of critical residues involved in the described XBP1u mechanism resulted in loss of stalling activity, however, one mutation (S255A) turned out to be enhancing. Notably, our saturation mutagenesis experiments demonstrate that the XBP1u AP has not evolved to maximize its resistance to pulling forces on the nascent chain, and that many more enhancing mutations exist.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis data.

claim: P254 plays a critical role in arrest potency, since nine other residues in this position can all impart stronger arrest potency on the AP.
source: P254 plays a critical role in this regard, since nine other residues in this position can all impart stronger arrest potency on the AP.
evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The large increase in translational arrest caused by the Q253N mutation points to a very specific requirement for size and hydrogen-bonding capacity in this position.
source: The large increase in translational arrest caused by the Q253N mutation (but no other mutation in this position) points to a very specific requirement for size and hydrogen-bonding capacity in this particular position in the AP.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis data.

claim: Stronger versions of the XBP1u AP can be useful as force sensors to study cotranslational processes.
source: Stronger versions of the XBP1u AP can be useful as force sensors to study cotranslational processes such as membrane-protein insertion into the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis results.

claim: The mildly hydrophobic HR2 segment of XBP1u is likely to be recognized as a canonical signal sequence by SRP.
source: We also found that the mildly hydrophobic HR2 segment of XBP1u is likely to be recognized as a canonical signal sequence by SRP, with clear density visible in the SRP54 M-domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cryo-EM structural observations.

claim: HR2 cannot engage productively with the Sec61 translocon as a signal sequence.
source: However, HR2 cannot engage productively with the Sec61 translocon as a signal sequence, which is consistent with previous reports of minimal membrane insertion observed for XBP1u HR2 (Plumb et al., 2015; Kanda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations and citations to Plumb et al., 2015; Kanda et al., 2016.

claim: The nascent chain conformation is unaltered within the tunnel in three distinct stages of ER targeting.
source: Finally, we observed that the nascent chain conformation is unaltered within the tunnel in three distinct stages of ER targeting of the ribosome-XBP1u complex: during ribosomal pausing, after recruitment of SRP and upon interaction with Sec61 translocon, arguing against the idea of a force-mediated release of translational stalling after targeting to the ER membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing three cryo-EM structures.

claim: The linker length between the pausing site and the beginning of the HR2 region may be responsible for uncoupling of HR2 interactions from arrest peptide conformation.
source: Independently of the nature of this interaction, however, the linker length between the pausing site and the beginning of the HR2 region of XBP1u may also be responsible for uncoupling of HR2 interactions from arrest peptide conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: The maximal accumulation of full-length product occurred at a linker length of 43 amino acids in force profile analysis.
source: From our force profile analysis, the maximal accumulation of full-length product (i.e. maximal force) occurred at a linker length of 43 amino acids, whereas in stalled XBP1u HR2 is around 52 amino acids distant from the PTC, and hence will hardly exert significant pulling force even if inserted into the ER membrane.
evidence: This is a result from force profile analysis.

claim: In stalled XBP1u, HR2 is around 52 amino acids distant from the PTC.
source: From our force profile analysis, the maximal accumulation of full-length product (i.e. maximal force) occurred at a linker length of 43 amino acids, whereas in stalled XBP1u HR2 is around 52 amino acids distant from the PTC, and hence will hardly exert significant pulling force even if inserted into the ER membrane.
evidence: This is determined from the structure and sequence.

claim: The XBP1u AP interaction with the ribosomal tunnel pauses ribosomes sufficiently for the mildly hydrophobic HR2 domain to gain competence for SRP recruitment.
source: Based on our findings, we propose a structural and mechanistic explanation of XBP1u's role in the UPR. The XBP1u AP interaction with the ribosomal tunnel pauses ribosomes sufficiently as for the mildly hydrophobic HR2 domain to gain competence for SRP recruitment.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural and functional data.

claim: The recruitment of SRP ensures proper co-translational targeting and localization of the XBP1u mRNA to the Sec61 translocon on the ER membrane.
source: The recruitment of SRP ensures proper co-translational targeting, and subsequent localization of the XBP1u mRNA, to the Sec61 translocon on the ER membrane, ensuring efficient cleavage of the XBP1u mRNA by IRE1α.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural and functional data.

claim: The observed unaltered states of the XBP1u nascent chain suggest that neither SRP nor Sec61 release the translation stall induced by the XBP1u AP.
source: The observed unaltered states of the XBP1u nascent chain within the ribosomal tunnel suggest that neither SRP nor Sec61 release the translation stall induced by the XBP1u AP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The pausing may resolve autonomously with the given short half-life.
source: If XBP1u-induced pausing is not released by force, we rather envision two alternative scenarios regarding the fate of the properly targeted, paused complex. First, the pausing may resolve autonomously with the given short half-life or, second, the paused complex is recognized by the Pelota/Hbs1 surveillance system as shown in yeast and recycled.
evidence: This is a proposed scenario based on inference.

claim: The paused complex may be recognized by the Pelota/Hbs1 surveillance system and recycled.
source: If XBP1u-induced pausing is not released by force, we rather envision two alternative scenarios regarding the fate of the properly targeted, paused complex. First, the pausing may resolve autonomously with the given short half-life or, second, the paused complex is recognized by the Pelota/Hbs1 surveillance system as shown in yeast and recycled.
evidence: This is a proposed scenario based on inference and knowledge from yeast.

claim: Autonomous resolution of pausing is more likely in vivo, since the wildtype XBP1u AP is even weaker than the S255A mutant.
source: The former is more likely in vivo, since the wildtype XBP1u AP is even weaker than the S255A mutant used in this study.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis data.

claim: The pause is released when incubated longer during in vitro translations.
source: In addition, it has also been shown biochemically that the pause is released when incubated longer during in vitro translations (Yanagitani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yanagitani et al., 2011.

claim: The pausing of XBP1u might have evolved as a precise timer for co-translational localization of its polysome-carrying mRNA on the ER membrane.
source: In conclusion, the pausing of XBP1u might have evolved as a precise timer, which can pause ribosomes temporarily in order to allow co-translational localization of its polysome-carrying mRNA on the ER membrane for efficient splicing by IRE1α.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary explanation based on all findings.

claim: The mild pausing phenotype is induced by a tight turn of the AP within the exit tunnel.
source: Interestingly, the mild pausing phenotype is induced by a tight turn of the AP within the exit tunnel, and mirrored by a rather minimal perturbation of the PTC through re-positioning of just one nucleotide, C4398.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The mild pausing phenotype is mirrored by a minimal perturbation of the PTC through re-positioning of just one nucleotide, C4398.
source: Interestingly, the mild pausing phenotype is induced by a tight turn of the AP within the exit tunnel, and mirrored by a rather minimal perturbation of the PTC through re-positioning of just one nucleotide, C4398.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.
